cls: Substituted benzamide; selective dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (with 5-HT4 agonism)
quick: 25 mg (1 tablet) three times daily before meals for dyspepsia; higher divided doses for psychiatric use
Take before meals (about 15-30 min before food)
Caution and consider dose reduction - eliminated mainly via urine
EPS/movement signs, prolactin-related symptoms, ECG/QT in at-risk patients
summary: Levosulpiride is the levo (L) enantiomer of sulpiride, a substituted benzamide that acts as a selective dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (with 5-HT4 agonist prokinetic activity). It is used short-term as a prokinetic for dyspeptic syndrome from delayed gastric emptying (e.g., diabetic gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia) and, at higher doses, as an antipsychotic/antidepressant in some countries (common in India, Italy, and Korea). Key risks are dopamine-blockade effects: extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, gynecomastia, menstrual changes), QT prolongation, and rarely neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is NOT FDA-approved - this record is built from EMA/SmPC and peer-reviewed sources and is PENDING CLINICAL REVIEW.
indications: Short-term treatment of dyspeptic syndrome (anorexia, bloating, epigastric tenderness, postprandial fullness, heartburn, belching) from delayed gastric emptying related to organic factors (e.g., diabetic gastroparesis) and/or functional factors, in patients who failed other therapy
Symptomatic short-term treatment of nausea and vomiting induced by anticancer drugs after failure of first-line therapy (per SmPC)
Symptomatic short-term treatment of dizziness, tinnitus, hearing loss and nausea associated with Meniere-type syndromes (per SmPC)
Antipsychotic / antidepressant use (e.g., schizophrenia, dysthymia) at higher doses in some national approvals

dosage.d: 25 mg (1 tablet) three times daily, before meals
dosage.n: Short-term use; per SmPC. Elderly: physician should consider a reduced dose

dosage.d: Typically 25-50 mg three times daily (commonly 50-150 mg/day)
dosage.n: Off-SmPC / regional; not an EMA prokinetic indication - use specialist guidance

dosage.d: Higher doses, typically 200-400 mg/day in divided doses
dosage.n: Regional psychiatric approvals only; titrate per specialist; higher EPS and prolactin risk

admin: Take by mouth before meals (about 15-30 minutes before food) to optimize the prokinetic effect
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration for the dyspeptic indication
Not recommended in children (no data in the prokinetic SmPC)
Review continued need regularly, particularly because of movement-disorder and prolactin risks
moa: Levosulpiride is the levo-enantiomer of sulpiride and carries the antidopaminergic activity of the racemate. It acts as a selective dopamine D2 receptor antagonist. Centrally, D2 blockade in mesolimbic pathways underlies its antipsychotic effect, while blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin and in nigrostriatal pathways produces extrapyramidal effects. In the gut it antagonizes inhibitory presynaptic dopamine D2 receptors and acts as a 5-HT4 receptor agonist, enhancing acetylcholine release and increasing gastric and gallbladder emptying and upper-GI motility (prokinetic effect).

absolute: Hypersensitivity to levosulpiride or any excipient
Manic states / manic phase of manic-depressive (bipolar) psychosis
Pheochromocytoma (risk of hypertensive crisis from catecholamine release)
Prolactin-dependent tumors and known malignant breast disease (mastopathy)
Conditions where increased GI motility could be harmful (GI bleeding, mechanical obstruction or perforation)
relative: History or risk factors for QT prolongation / cardiac disease
Risk factors for stroke / cerebrovascular events (elderly with dementia)
Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders
Galactose intolerance / lactase deficiency (tablets contain lactose)
monitor: Extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of tardive dyskinesia
Serum prolactin and prolactin-related symptoms with prolonged use
ECG/QT interval and electrolytes in at-risk patients
Temperature, rigidity and mental status (neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

preg: Contraindicated per the SmPC; there are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnancy. Neonates exposed to antipsychotics (including levosulpiride) during the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder) and should be carefully monitored. Do not use in pregnancy or possible pregnancy.
lact: Contraindicated during breastfeeding per the SmPC. Like other dopamine antagonists it raises prolactin and may be excreted in milk; avoid use while breastfeeding.
renal: Levosulpiride is eliminated mainly unchanged via the urine, so exposure increases when renal function is reduced. Use with caution and consider a reduced dose / lower frequency in renal impairment.
hepatic: Limited specific data; the drug is predominantly renally eliminated rather than extensively hepatically metabolized. Use with caution in hepatic impairment and apply the general principle of lowest effective dose.

major: Levodopa and dopamine agonists - mutual antagonism; levosulpiride opposes their antiparkinsonian effect (avoid co-use)
Other QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, other antipsychotics, methadone, certain macrolides/fluoroquinolones) - additive risk of arrhythmia/torsades
Other neuroleptics / antipsychotics - additive EPS and NMS risk; avoid concomitant neuroleptics
moderate: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedatives, hypnotics) - additive sedation
Anticholinergic drugs, narcotics and analgesics - antagonize the prokinetic/GI-motility effect
Other psychotropic drugs - require special caution to avoid unwanted interactions
minor: Drugs whose absorption depends on gastric motility/emptying may be affected by the prokinetic action
interactions.food: Take before meals; the prokinetic effect is intended to precede food
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum prolactin, which can confound endocrine testing and interfere with imaging that uses some dopaminergic agents

common: Hyperprolactinemia and related symptoms with prolonged use
serious: Extrapyramidal symptoms - parkinsonism, dyskinesia, tremor, dystonia, akathisia
Venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis)
Increased risk of cerebrovascular events in elderly patients with dementia
rare: Ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperpyrexia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness)
Neonatal withdrawal / extrapyramidal syndrome after third-trimester exposure
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome - high fever, severe rigidity, altered consciousness
Ventricular arrhythmia / torsades de pointes / cardiac arrest / sudden death

monitoring: Watch for extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia, especially with prolonged or high-dose use
Serum prolactin and prolactin-related symptoms (galactorrhea, menstrual disturbance, gynecomastia) with prolonged therapy
ECG/QT interval and serum electrolytes in patients with cardiac risk or interacting drugs
Temperature, muscle rigidity and mental status for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Signs of venous thromboembolism in at-risk patients
counsel: Take before meals, about 15-30 minutes before food
Avoid alcohol while on this medicine
Report abnormal movements, muscle stiffness, restlessness, breast milk discharge, breast swelling, or menstrual changes
Seek urgent care for high fever with stiffness/confusion, palpitations or fainting, or sudden breathlessness/chest pain
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially other antipsychotics, levodopa, and heart-rhythm drugs
May cause drowsiness - use caution when driving or operating machinery, especially at higher doses
Note: this medicine is not FDA-approved - follow local prescribing guidance
pk: Prokinetic effect over the dosing interval; full clinical benefit may take days of regular use
Peak plasma concentration about 1.5-2 hours after oral dosing
No special storage precautions required; store in original blister, protect from moisture (per SmPC)
pearls: Levosulpiride is the active L-enantiomer of sulpiride and carries its antidopaminergic activity; it has dual prokinetic action via D2 antagonism plus 5-HT4 agonism
Eliminated mainly unchanged in urine, so renal impairment increases exposure - reduce dose accordingly
Dopamine D2 blockade explains both the therapeutic and adverse profile: EPS, tardive dyskinesia, and prominent hyperprolactinemia
Contraindicated in pheochromocytoma (hypertensive crisis - treat with phentolamine), epilepsy, mania, and prolactin-dependent / breast tumors
Not FDA-approved; widely used in India, Italy, and Korea under EMA/national formularies
missed: If you miss a dose, take it before your next meal if you remember in time; otherwise skip it and resume your usual schedule before the next meal. Do not take two doses together to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may theoretically produce extrapyramidal effects and sleep/CNS disturbances; at very high doses, sedation, dystonia, and QT prolongation/arrhythmia are possible. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with ECG and vital-sign monitoring; discontinue or reduce the dose, treat extrapyramidal reactions with antiparkinsonian (anticholinergic) agents, and manage arrhythmias and neuroleptic malignant syndrome supportively.
